title: Lab 1 - Explore a real cluster's architecture
description: Build a three-node cluster and inspect every control plane component from the inside: static Pod manifests, etcd health, scheduler decisions and node conditions.
scenario:
You have just joined a team that runs Kubernetes and nobody can tell you how the cluster is actually put together. Rather than reading a diagram, you are going to open the cluster up and confirm every component for yourself: where the control plane manifests live, which process supervises them, how the scheduler explains its decisions, and what a node reports about its own health.

By the end you should be able to answer 'what is running where, and who started it' for any cluster you are dropped into.
environment_setup:
# 1. Create a three-node kind cluster
cat <<'EOF' > kind-cka.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: cka
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker
EOF

kind create cluster --config kind-cka.yaml

# 2. Confirm the cluster is up
kubectl get nodes
kubectl cluster-info

# You should see one control-plane node and two workers, all Ready.
cleanup:
kind delete cluster --name cka
rm -f kind-cka.yaml

tasks.title: Task 1 - Identify every control plane component
tasks.instructions: List the Pods running in the kube-system namespace and identify which ones belong to the control plane, which are networking components, and which are addons. Note which node each one runs on.
tasks.solution:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide

# Filter to just the control plane:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l tier=control-plane

# Control plane: kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager
#   -> all on the control-plane node only
# Networking:    kube-proxy (one per node, a DaemonSet), kindnet (CNI)
# Addons:        coredns (a Deployment, usually 2 replicas)
tasks.verification:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'apiserver|etcd|scheduler|controller-manager'
# All four should be Running on the control-plane node.

tasks.title: Task 2 - Find the static Pod manifests
tasks.instructions: The control plane Pods are not created by any controller. Get a shell on the control plane node, find the directory holding their manifests, and identify which process is watching that directory.
tasks.solution:
docker exec -it cka-control-plane bash

ls -l /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

# The kubelet watches this directory:
ps aux | grep kubelet | head -1
# Look for --pod-manifest-path, or check the kubelet config:
grep -i staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests

exit
tasks.verification:
docker exec cka-control-plane ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# Four YAML files listed.

tasks.title: Task 3 - Read the API server's configuration
tasks.instructions: Extract the kube-apiserver command-line flags. Find the authorisation modes in use, the etcd endpoints it connects to, and the path to the client CA certificate.
tasks.solution:
docker exec cka-control-plane grep -A40 'command:' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Or from the running Pod:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '\n'

# Look for:
#   --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
#   --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
#   --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
tasks.verification:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep authorization-mode

tasks.title: Task 4 - Check etcd health with etcdctl
tasks.instructions: Using the certificates referenced by the etcd static Pod manifest, run an endpoint health check and list the cluster members. Do this from inside the etcd container.
tasks.solution:
kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-cka-control-plane -- sh -c '
  ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
    endpoint health'

# And the member list:
kubectl -n kube-system exec -it etcd-cka-control-plane -- sh -c '
  ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
    member list -w table'

# Note the certificate paths - they came straight out of etcd.yaml.
# You will use this exact command shape for backups in Phase 4.
tasks.verification: # The health check prints: https://127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy

tasks.title: Task 5 - Watch the scheduler make a decision
tasks.instructions: Create a Pod and observe, through events, that it was scheduled and onto which node. Then create a Pod that cannot be scheduled and read the scheduler's explanation.
tasks.solution:
# A Pod that schedules normally
kubectl run schedulable --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pod schedulable -o wide
kubectl describe pod schedulable | grep -A5 Events
# Normal  Scheduled  default-scheduler  Successfully assigned default/schedulable to cka-worker

# A Pod that cannot possibly be scheduled
kubectl run impossible --image=nginx --restart=Never \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"disktype":"nvme-that-does-not-exist"}}}'

kubectl get pod impossible
# STATUS: Pending

kubectl describe pod impossible | grep -A5 Events
# Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler
#   0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.

# Fix it by labelling a node:
kubectl label node cka-worker disktype=nvme-that-does-not-exist
kubectl get pod impossible -w   # it schedules within seconds
tasks.verification:
kubectl get pods -o wide
# Both Pods should eventually be Running on a worker node.

tasks.title: Task 6 - Read node conditions and capacity
tasks.instructions: For one worker node, report its conditions, its allocatable CPU and memory, and the total resources requested by the Pods already on it.
tasks.solution:
kubectl describe node cka-worker

# The three sections that matter:
kubectl describe node cka-worker | grep -A8 'Conditions:'
# MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure should be False; Ready should be True

kubectl describe node cka-worker | grep -A6 'Allocatable:'

kubectl describe node cka-worker | grep -A8 'Allocated resources:'
# Shows Requests and Limits as a percentage of allocatable

# As structured output:
kubectl get node cka-worker -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}' | tr ',' '\n'

tasks.title: Task 7 - Break the scheduler and observe the effect
tasks.instructions: Temporarily stop the scheduler by moving its static Pod manifest aside. Create a Pod and confirm what happens. Then restore the manifest and confirm recovery. This is the single most instructive exercise in the lab.
tasks.solution:
# Move the manifest out of the watched directory
docker exec cka-control-plane mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/

# Within ~20 seconds the scheduler Pod disappears
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler

# Now create a Pod
kubectl run orphan --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pod orphan
# STATUS: Pending - forever, with no FailedScheduling event at all,
# because nothing is even looking at it.

kubectl describe pod orphan | grep -A5 Events
# <none>  -- note the absence of any scheduler message. That absence IS the clue.

# Restore it
docker exec cka-control-plane mv /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# The kubelet restarts the scheduler and the pending Pod is placed
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler
kubectl get pod orphan -w
tasks.verification:
kubectl get pod orphan -o wide
# Should now be Running with a node assigned.

tasks.title: Task 8 - Trace a request end to end
tasks.instructions: Create a Deployment and, using only events and object inspection, write down the ownership chain from Pod back to Deployment, plus the node each Pod landed on.
tasks.solution:
kubectl create deployment trace --image=nginx --replicas=2

# The chain, top down
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=trace -o wide

# The chain, bottom up, from a Pod
POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=trace -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl get pod $POD -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}/{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'
# ReplicaSet/trace-xxxxxxxxx

RS=$(kubectl get pod $POD -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}')
kubectl get rs $RS -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}/{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'
# Deployment/trace

# The events, in order
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep trace
tasks.verification:
kubectl get deploy trace
# READY should be 2/2
